title: Trump declines to call for Max Miller’s resignation amid abuse allegations – live
summary: President says he will ‘let the families figure that out’ and calls situation ‘a very sad thing’ when asked if Ohio Republican should step down
body: The US House of Representatives ethics committee on Monday recommended that Chuck Edwards, a Republican congressman, face censure after determining he “fostered a hostile work environment and engaged in sexual harassment” by giving gifts and lavishing attention on two young female staffers. The bipartisan panel began investigating the second-term North Carolina congressman earlier this year, after receiving complaints about his conduct. In their report, they determined Edwards broke House rules by singling out the two unidentified aides for special treatment that made them uncomfortable and harmed relations with other employees. While the investigation uncovered no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with the staffers or suggested it, his behavior violated provisions in the House code of conduct that prohibit sexual harassment and unwanted advances. The congressman “acknowledged at least some of the behavior at issue could be viewed as inappropriate”, but “has not acknowledged or taken responsibility for the harm he caused”, the committee wrote in its report. A compromise between Todd Blanche and two Republican senators that potentially cleared the way for Blanche’s confirmation as attorney general is weak, Democrats and several experts said, as it makes promises Donald Trump can easily reverse. Blanche, the acting attorney general, posted two documents on Sunday evening showing he was withdrawing an 18 May order allowing for the creation of a $1.8bn weaponization fund and clarifying that broad tax immunity the justice department granted to Trump only applied retroactively to the president, his sons, and businesses. The agreement stemmed from a deal worked out with senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, two Republicans who had threatened to block Blanche’s nomination. Cornyn and Tillis said on Monday they would support Blanche when his vote comes up for the Senate judiciary committee Tuesday. “We are pleased that the Department of Justice has issued a formal order terminating the anti-weaponization fund,” Cornyn and Tillis said. “Additionally, the department has acknowledged in a binding written order that the audit settlement is limited to the plaintiffs and the scope does not extend beyond the defendants in the lawsuit, the IRS and the treasury, addressing concerns that multiple of our Republican colleagues share.” But legal experts and Democrats said what Blanche announced Sunday was far from ironclad and left room for Trump to resurrect the fund. “These assurances are not worth the paper they’re written on,” Brandon DeBot, policy director at the Tax Law Center at NYU, said in a statement. “They don’t pull back on the ongoing attempts to give the president, his family, and his affiliates unauthorized immunity from tax audits. They don’t do anything new to stop the president from trying to bring back the fund, as he threatened to this weekend. It’s abundantly clear we need congressional action.” A group of 25 states sued the Trump administration over a round of tariffs that went into effect last month, arguing that the US president exceeded his legal authority to tax imports after the US supreme court struck down his previous set of global tariffs. “President Trump is so intent on raising the cost of living for Americans that he is willing to break law after law after law to do so,” said California attorney general Rob Bonta in a statement. “Tariffs are taxes, and the American people cannot and should not shoulder the extra costs that come from the President’s failed and illegal economic policy — no matter how much the President wants them to.” The lawsuit challenges tariffs of 10% to 12.5% imposed on dozens of countries, including the UK, Mexico, Canada, Australia, India, China and the 27 countries that make up the European Union, which took effect on 24 July. The Trump administration said it imposed the tariffs in an effort to stop exports of goods produced with forced labor. But states argue the latest measures are an unlawful attempt to replace tariffs the courts have repeatedly rejected. In February, the US supreme court declared many of Trump’s tariffs illegal in a 6-3 ruling, deciding that a 1977 law designed to address national emergencies did not provide the legal justification for most of the Trump administration’s tariffs. In May, the US court of international trade ruled in favor of small businesses that challenged the tariffs. Ahead of a vote by the senate judiciary committee on whether to advance Todd Blanche’s nomination to become US attorney general, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer attacked Blanche, saying he has “no intention of stopping Trump’s corruption,” adding that he has instead “spent his career enabling it.” Amid threats from two Republican senators to block Blanche’s confirmation, Blanche rescinded his establishment of Trump’s “anti-weaponization fund.” John Cornyn and Thom Tillis said they would advance with their nomination. Addressing this, Schumer said: “Instead of seeing Todd Blanche’s so-called deal for the sham that it is, Senate Republicans are once again taking Trump’s personal attorney at his word.” “Blanche is still perfectly fine giving Trump a permission slip to commit tax fraud to the tune of millions of dollars,” Schumer added. “Is the GOP willing to go along with it?” Senate judiciary committee chair Chuck Grassley has asked Jack Smith, the former special counsel behind the criminal cases against Donald Trump, to appear before the committee on 22 September, according to an invitation reviewed by Politico. The request follows months of scrutiny from Grassley’s team into Smith and the investigations he oversaw. Smith is the former federal prosecutor tapped by the justice department to lead inquiries into Trump’s handling of classified documents and his attempts to overturn the 2020 election, cases that were dropped after Trump’s 2024 election win. He testified before the House judiciary committee back in January. Representative Daniel Goldman, who was absolutely crushed in his re-election bid for his New York seat by Brad Lander, said representative Ro Khanna from California’s opinion was “wrong” that an “unfair political and economy system” is what drove progressive victories in House democratic primaries. “All three of us who lost in NYC had very progressive records (including supporting Medicare for All) and we all had the overwhelming support of actual working families — labor unions, public housing residents and immigrant communities,” Goldman wrote. “That’s because we all have gone to battle for those communities and offered practical and meaningful solutions that could actually get passed in a system that requires bipartisanship.” “The voters in my district prioritized a different issue, and I respect their decision,” Goldman wrote, implying that his pro-Israel stance had been his electoral downfall. On Sunday, Max Miller’s ex father-in-law and Ohio senator Bernie Moreno issued a public statement against Miller, calling for his resignation. In his statement, Moreno said that the “last two years have been pure hell for my wife Bridget, our daughter Emily, me, and our entire family in the aftermath of Emily’s divorce.” Addressing reports of the abuse allegations as well as the public scrunity, Moreno said: “It has been horrific to watch this play out in full public view, all while knowing an innocent two-year-old girl is caught in the middle… Out of concern for the safety of my family, I hoped to keep this matter private but Max Miller’s increasingly erratic and dangerous behavior has made that impossible.” He went on to join calls of resignation against Miller, saying: “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them. He should not serve in the House of Representatives. I believe Max Miller needs to seek professional help to end the clear pattern of abuse he has left in his wake. I believe he should not be free to continue endangering others until he does.” Trump’s refusal to call for Max Miller’s resignation comes amid heightened scrutiny into the Ohio representative’s abuse allegations. The Republican congressman, 37, who represents Ohio’s seventh congressional district, has denied accusations made by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, and former girlfriend Stephanie Grisham, as he campaigns for re-election. On Sunday, Miller doubled down on his denial, saying: “I’m not getting out of this race, and I’m winning in November.” Moreno, a conservative policy adviser, shares a two-year-old daughter with Miller. The pair have been engaged in a legal battle over custody of their child since 2024. In one alleged incident, Miller “took hot water from a pan he had just cooked eggs in and threw it at me”, Moreno testified earlier this year amid a defamation lawsuit Miller filed against her. Moreno has also accused Miller of holding a gun to her head, the New York Times reported. The pair married in 2022. Separately, Miller’s former girlfriend Grisham, who served as White House press secretary during Donald Trump’s first administration, has also accused him of abuse, an allegation he has denied. Grisham and Miller dated from 2019 to 2020. In a 2021 Washington Post op-ed, Grisham – without naming Miller – wrote about a relationship that “turned abusive”, and of a former partner who was “physical” with her. Although she did not identify Miller in the article, he said it was widely understood that the op-ed referred to him. She later confirmed she was talking about Miller, according to the Times. In the most contentious part of the press conference, Trump lashed out at US Attorney Jeanine Pirro for dropping charges against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn, who was accused of vandalizing the newly renovated Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. “I was disappointed with Jeanine Pirro. title: US states sue Trump administration over new tariffs on 60 trading partners
summary: Coalition of 25 states asks US Court of International Trade to halt tariffs and declare them them unlawful
body: A coalition of 25 US states sued the Trump administration on Monday over new tariffs pegged at 10% to 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners, calling them a pretext for replacing import taxes struck down by the supreme court in February. The states are asking the US Court of International Trade to halt the tariffs, declare them unlawful and order refunds of duties that have already been paid. According to the states involved in the action, tariffs on 59 countries and the European Union imposed last month account for 99.4% of US imports. The Trump administration officials have charged that the countries have not done enough to crack down on imports produced by forced labor. “After losing at the Supreme Court, the administration is once again trying to illegally raise taxes on families and businesses with a new round of tariffs,” New York attorney general Letitia James said in a statement. “No matter how the administration tries to justify it, the law and our Constitution are clear that the president does not have the power to impose sweeping tariffs on whatever countries he wants,” James added. In addition to New York, the states joining the action are Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Washington and Wisconsin, along with the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania. The new tariffs went into effect in July after “Liberation Day” tariffs were ruled unconstitutional in February and a new set of temporary tariffs expired. The latest proposal for tariffs uses Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a federal law meant to target countries that use forced labor. The new tariffs affect major trading partners including Canada, Japan, Norway, Taiwan and China. The lawsuit follows a separate suit filed by the Liberty Justice Center on behalf of two US small businesses who argue that Trump exceeded his executive authority with the new tariffs. “The United States is using its lawful authority to obtain the elimination of unreasonable acts, policies, and practices that burden US commerce,” White House spokesman Kush Desai said. “A foreign country’s failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor is unreasonable and burdens US commerce, including American workers, and must be addressed. Section 301 tariffs have proven to be a legally durable tool since the President’s first term, and they remain so now.” The New York governor, Kathy Hochul, and the state attorney general argue that the administration’s tariffs based on “a supposed investigation into countries’ efforts to combat forced labor do not satisfy the requirements of Section 301”, they said in a statement. They said that the administration is using “forced labor” as an excuse to continue its policy of indiscriminately enacting damaging tariffs on a wide range of countries that lead to higher prices for their constituents. “President Trump’s illegal tariffs are nothing more than a tax on hardworking families, driving up the cost of groceries, household essentials, building materials, and countless everyday goods that New Yorkers rely on,” Hochul said. “The Supreme Court has made it clear that this administration cannot ignore the law to impose sweeping tariffs.”

title: Trump accuses Jeanine Pirro of ‘folding’ by dropping reflecting pool charges
summary: Trump ‘disappointed’ with US attorney amid reports he’s considering removing her from her post
body: Donald Trump accused US attorney Jeanine Pirro of having “folded like an umbrella” amid reports that he was considering removing her from her post. Trump criticized Pirro on Monday after she dropped vandalism charges against a former Olympian accused of damaging the recently renovated Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool. Trump nominated Pirro to serve as interim US attorney for the District of Columbia last year, and the Senate later confirmed her in August. Speaking to reporters from the Oval Office, Trump said: “Frankly, I think she choked because the judge was really vicious. Instead of going after the people that did it, the judge went after her and went after her department, and I guess she choked,” appearing to refer to DC superior court judge Todd Edelman who is overseeing the vandalism case. He added: “I was disappointed with Jeanine Pirro, really disappointed with Jeanine Pirro. She folded like an umbrella.” Trump refused to answer a follow-up question from a reporter on whether he is reconsidering her role, instead saying: “You’re fake news. Don’t ever talk again.” Last Friday, the justice department dismissed the criminal case against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn, one of seven people charged in connection with what Trump claimed were attempts to vandalize the $15m renovation of the reflecting pool. Hearn had faced a felony property destruction charge that carried a potential sentence of up to 10 years in prison and a $1,000 fine. He pleaded not guilty last month. According to the justice department last week, the damage to the pool liner came as “the result of flawed installation by the contractor”. Pirro said her office received documents from the interior department only “after the return of the indictment” that showed the pool was already damaged before Hearn touched the water on 19 June. A motion by government lawyers said that documents “indicated a rushed and flawed installation process, with repeated failures of the lining during the installation process, and extensive peeling of the lining throughout the Reflecting Pool”. Pirro’s office said “it was not until after these documents were produced” that it “first became aware of information showing that the damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism as initially represented by DOI.” Trump’s public attacks against Pirro on Monday follows his Truth Social post over the weekend in which he said: “I disagree 100% with Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, on the Reflecting Pool. I don’t know what she was thinking? To me, it was a pure case of VANDALISM.” Speaking to CNN, one person familiar with the matter said that Trump is “furious” with Pirro and that they think it is “highly likely she’s removed from her job”. Meanwhile, one senior administration official told the outlet that Trump was “blindsided” by Pirro’s decision, adding: “The president did not know beforehand that she was going to do that.” The Guardian has reached out to the White House and the justice department for comment.

title: Ukrainian drone attacks on Black Sea resort and Crimea kill 11, Russia claims
summary: Seven people, including three children, dead after ‘drone debris’ strike beach in seaside town, says Russian taskforce
body: Ukrainian drone attacks on a Black Sea resort and the annexed Crimea peninsula killed 11 people, Russian officials said after blaming Ukraine for another explosion that killed five people in a Moscow restaurant. Seven people, including three children, were killed when “drone debris” struck a beach in the seaside town of Arkhipo-Osipovka, the crisis taskforce for Russia’s southern Krasnodar region said on social media. Social media videos, verified by Reuters and the BBC, showed tourists in the water and on the shore watching on as what appeared to be a drone slammed into a busy beach. Another four people were killed in a Ukrainian strike on the illegally annexed Crimea, the Moscow-installed governor, Sergey Aksyonov, said in a post on Telegram. Both Crimea and the Black Sea coast are popular holiday destinations for Russian tourists during summer. Earlier, Russia blamed Ukraine for a bombing at a restaurant in central Moscow that killed five people, amid growing speculation that a senior Russian military commander was the intended target. The explosion occurred on Saturday evening near the entrance to an upmarket Italian restaurant in one of the city’s seven Stalin-era skyscrapers on Kudrinskaya Square. Russian prosecutors said an unidentified woman carrying an improvised explosive device had attempted to enter the restaurant but was stopped by a security guard. The device detonated moments later, killing five people and injuring 19 others. In a statement on Sunday, Russia’s foreign ministry accused Kyiv of carrying out the attack, saying: “The bloody tentacles of [Volodymyr] Zelenskyy’s terrorist gang have reached the Balzi Rossi Italian restaurant in Moscow.” Russian authorities have not identified the intended target or named the victims. However, pro-Kremlin military bloggers and several independent Russian media outlets reported that the attack may have been aimed at Col Gen Alexander Chaiko, the commander of Russia’s aerospace forces, who was reportedly attending a private banquet at the restaurant to celebrate his 55th birthday. Photographs and videos that appeared online shortly after the bombing, purportedly from the private event, showed a stage with the words “Aleksandr 55” displayed in the background. Chaiko is one of Russia’s top military commanders, having led the failed assault on Kyiv in early 2022 before later being promoted to command the Russian air force. The Telegram channel VChK-OGPU, which is known for publishing leaks from within Russia’s security services, reported that Chaiko escaped unharmed. According to the channel, his daughter, Maria, was seriously injured in the blast, while her husband, Daniil Peredriy, was killed. They were outside on the restaurant’s terrace when the explosion occurred. The Russian newspaper Kommersant reported that investigators believed the woman carrying the explosive device may not have known she was transporting a bomb, suggesting it was detonated remotely by another person, killing her. Among the other reported victims was a member of Russia’s elite Federal Protective Service (FSO). Kyiv has not yet commented on the incidents. Both sides have repeatedly said they do not target civilians in the conflict, which is now in its fifth year. In Ukraine, one person was killed and dozens more injured when Russian planes launched a 90-minute bombing blitz on residential districts in the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, the regional chief, Ivan Fedorov, said on Monday. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s intelligence agencies have targeted dozens of senior Russian military officers and Russia-installed officials, accusing them of involvement in war crimes. Ukrainian intelligence services have previously employed a range of tactics, relying on both willing saboteurs and unwitting civilians to carry out bombings. They have succeeded in killing at least four Russian generals and several other senior military figures, as well as pro-war activists deep inside Russian territory, although some operations have missed their intended targets. In 2022, a car bomb killed Darya Dugina, the daughter of the ultranationalist Russian ideologue Aleksandr Dugin, in an attack widely believed to have been intended for her father.

title: Trump claims strait of Hormuz could open ‘by tomorrow’ as Iran denies any talks taking place – as it happened
summary: US president claims talks are ‘not very complex’ as he speaks at White House as Iran’s foreign ministry says there are no talks taking place with US
body: New talks between Washington and Tehran are the “last chance” for Iran to forge a deal and avoid an escalation of US strikes on the country, Donald Trump said on Monday. It comes a day after the US president again said he had called off further “massive strikes” because Gulf allies had urged diplomacy. It’s all very consistent with Trump’s repeated pattern over the last five months as he struggles to find an off-ramp; he threatens devastating military action, only to pull back at the last minute and claim the two sides are on the brink of an agreement to end the war. As my colleague Patrick Wintour notes, this is thought to be the 12th time in the war that Trump has called off threatened strikes. Indeed, Trump said he expected negotiations to begin in the next day or two to reopen the strait and create a pathway for Iran to address the US’s concerns about its nuclear programme. “The first phase is the opening of the straits. The second phase will be the denuclearization,” he told reporters in the Oval Office. “And that will take a little while.” He also reiterated that he was running out of patience with Iran, saying “this the last chance for them to sign a good document.” However, Tehran had on Monday denied that talks with the US were taking place. Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, told reporters at a weekly press briefing on Monday that Iran is not currently holding any talks with the US – contradicting claims made by Trump on Sunday night that talks with Iran would happen the next day. Baghaei said that there were no plans to receive a delegation or send an Iranian one, and that Iran’s current focus was on negotiations with Oman over the strait of Hormuz. “We are now going to reach an understanding on a route acceptable to both sides – neither the northern route nor the southern route – but one that respects the sovereign rights of both sides and safeguards our national interests and security,” he said in an interview with Iranian state television. To that, the US president called the Iranian leadership “unbelievably duplicitous” in a post on social media. He wrote on Truth Social: “They ask for a meeting, some would say ‘beg’, talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they’re not having any discussions, that nothing is being talked about, and they’re only dealing with ‘Oman’.” The Donald Trump doctrine has always contained a tenuous relationship with the truth. It was his mentor, the infamous New York lawyer Roy Cohn, who taught the young real estate mogul always to claim victory and never to admit defeat. Unfortunately for Trump, in Iran the US president has found a counterpart just as stubborn as himself. As Trump claims new negotiations are to begin with Tehran this week, Iran has shown it can also reignite the conflict by lobbing ballistic missiles at US bases in the region and maintaining a stranglehold on the strait of Hormuz, effectively taking initiative in the stalled peace process. And time is of the essence for Trump as the clock ticks toward a global energy crisis and a painful midterm elections for him and his Republican party. But as soon as his latest attempt to hammer out a peace deal was announced, it was denied by Iran and the US president was left fuming once again. Trump has suggested dozens of times since the beginning of the war that a deal with Iran is imminent, and his latest claim that new negotiations could produce a peace deal within days has shown the administration’s desperation to reopen the strait and find a road map out of the crisis. After promising to hit Iran “very hard”, Trump made a U-turn on Sunday and claimed that talks would continue and that the “perimeters of a deal” for the opening of Hormuz and the “denuclearization of Iran” had been agreed. Unfortunately, the Iranians don’t agree. In a statement on Monday, an Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson denied any peace negotiations were taking place. “We are not currently negotiating with the United States,” said Esmaeil Baqaei. “Our negotiations are with Oman to secure passage through the strait of Hormuz.” That may result in an agreement. But that will not result in the return of the strait of Hormuz to its prewar status, Baqaei added, in effect keeping the waterway a political football for the foreseeable future. “We must ensure that the strait of Hormuz cannot be misused by parties that have committed aggression against Iran,” said Baqaei. Little has changed since the last round of negotiations. Iran remains capable of closing the strait of Hormuz and stifling shipping – including a fifth of global oil supply – through the crucial waterway. The US remains capable of inflicting devastating strikes on Iran – despite a shortage of key munitions that could be needed for a war against key rivals like China – but has a lack of meaningful targets that could force Iran to change its policy. The Trump administration has been signalling a desire to end the conflict since April and three ceasefires have come and collapsed since then. With just over three months left until the US midterm elections, in which the Republicans are expected to lose the House and possibly even the Senate, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll last week showed that fewer than a third of Americans support the war in Iran, and 69% believe that Trump has not “clearly explained the goals of US military involvement in Iran”. For Iran, the strategic unpredictability has become a new weapon in a war that has counterintuitively strengthened its negotiating position, giving the regime new tools in slowing global oil supply and in attacking regional US allies in the Gulf. Iran has concluded that its best strategy is to “maximise the pain that they can impose on the United States and its partners in the region”, said Alex Vatanka, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute and an expert on Middle East security issues with a focus on Iran, during the institute’s podcast last week. The view there was that Trump “is not really yet ready for a deal with Iran, not a deal that would work for the Iranians anyway”. Iran is also facing a time crunch with a US blockade in effect halting trade out of the country. “They are now at a point where they don’t think just sitting back and having one round after another of diplomatic talks is the best way forward,” he added. “They’re trying to shake things up to try get Trump’s attention and see if they can get a different result.” Speaking in the Oval Office earlier, Trump also said that major oil companies are making “too much money” due to high prices stemming from his war on Iran, as he seeks to address his party’s political vulnerability ahead of the US midterm elections in November. “I don’t like it. They’re making too much money, okay? Based on a shortage, they’re making too much money. I don’t like it, and I should be the last one to say because I’m a big free enterprise guy,” he said. “Nobody bigger, and you know, you’re going to see oil when we’re finished with Iran. You’re going to see the prices drop through the floor. But they made too much money, too much money. Chevron, too much money. Exxon Mobil, too much, too much money.” High gasoline prices are a key political issue for Trump as his Republican Party heads into the midterms, with Democrats seeking to wrest control of Congress from them. The average price of a gallon of regular gasoline in the United States is up more than 37% since the start of the war, launched by Trump and Israel in late February. The war has seen Iran’s retaliatory action target Washington’s allies in the Gulf and virtually block the vital strait of Hormuz, with both moves sending energy prices skyrocketing. US petroleum giants ExxonMobil and Chevron released blowout profits on Friday, reflecting a major lift from the war that easily offset negative effects at both companies. ExxonMobil’s second-quarter profits more than doubled to $14.5bn, while Chevron’s came in at $12.1bn, more than five times the level in the year-ago quarter. Other major oil companies have also reported massive profits on the back of the war. Trump, a strong supporter of fossil fuel interests, has lashed out over prices at the pump, announcing in June that he was directing the US Department of Justice to investigate any “gouging” perpetrated by the industry. On Monday, he slammed the oil companies for their profits, saying he was “not happy about it”: When you look at one company where they made 12 times what they made the year before, they ought to give some of that back to the public, and they better cut the retail price, the consumer price. Too much money. You surprised I’m saying it. I’ll say it loud and clear. I’m not happy about it. With Agence-France Press. Donald Trump also said that newly planned talks with Tehran – which again, Iran has denied – are the “last chance” for Tehran to forge a deal and avoid an escalation of US strikes on the country. The US president reiterated that he’s running out of patience, telling reporters: We are talking right now [with Iran] at the request of Iran, backed by Saudi Arabia, backed by the UAE, and backed by Qatar in particular, but others also. Many countries called … but if it doesn’t happen, this is the last chance for them to sign a good document. Earlier, Trump also claimed – as he has in the past – that it was Iran who made contact with his administration to relaunch peace talks. He said: They called me and they said, please don’t attack. We’ll make a deal. That’s the real truth. And everyone knows it. And who wouldn’t call? One journalist in the Oval Office asked Trump what was different about this pause in airstrikes to previous occasions. Here was his response: I think we’re going to maybe get something, but I want to give them every last chance before decapitation. It’s very tough to do what I – what we – have planned. Still planned. We’ll see what happens. But it’s very, very tough thing to do. I t…

title: Far-right Republican accused of stiffing student debate champion of $8,000
summary: Briana Whatley sues Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback for unpaid scholarship from company he founded
body: A far-right Republican candidate in Florida’s governor’s race has been accused of stiffing a high school debate champion over the better part of $11,000 in scholarship money she won from a company he founded. Student Briana Whatley landed the awards as regional and national champion of Incubate Debate, a league-style competition set up by the candidate, James Fishback, to encourage youth to engage in political discourse. A recording posted to Substack by Fishback in May 2024 shows Whatley, now a second-year history student at Florida State University, accepting a $10,000 check for besting seven other finalists in the 2024 Incubate Debate national championship, adding to two $500 area awards she previously won. According to Florida Politics, Whatley is suing Fishback for not delivering $8,000 of the money that a letter from the company promised would be paid to her in full on the day she graduated high school in May last year. The filing names Incubate Foundation Inc, the parent of Incubate Debate, and Fishback, 31, who is challenging front-running US congressman Byron Donalds, and Jay Collins, the lieutenant governor of Florida, for the Republican nomination for state governor in November. The candidates face off in an 18 August primary. Whatley’s lawsuit, seen by the Guardian, was filed in small claims court in Broward county, where both she and Fishback went to school. Among the allegations are that Incubate Debate initially failed to respond to emails asking where the money was, then tried to change the terms of how it would be paid to her. Fishback, it said, “personally evaded and defrauded Plaintiff by initially ignoring communications, later blaming a terminated employee for the written award terms, falsely claiming an unwritten ‘installment policy,’ and delaying payment for months”. The document said Fishback admitted he “totally dropped the ball on this one” in a November 2025 text asking her to resend her bank details, then in December paid only $3,000 via Zelle. In another text, Fishback allegedly claimed that the employee who sent the original award letter promising payment in full on graduation had been fired, and that installment payments had “always been the case”, despite no previous mention of it. The text exchanges indicate a previously cordial relationship between the pair, with Fishback calling Whatley “a star”, and the student thanking him for “wanting to make it right”. Whatley claims Fishback broke off communication five months ago after she questioned why a promised 1 February installment was not paid. She is suing for the outstanding $8,000 plus interest and costs, and a pretrial conference is scheduled for 9 September. Whatley, the lawsuit said, has “suffered severe financial injury and out-of-pocket damages” as a result of Fishback’s alleged failure to pay. The Guardian has contacted Fishback for comment. In a court ruling last week, Fishback survived a legal challenge by Collins to remove him from this month’s primary. A judge in Tallahassee ruled that Fishback had not violated a rule requiring a gubernatorial candidate to be a resident of the state for seven years prior to the election, even though he bought a condo in Washington DC in 2020 that he declared his primary residence, and voted there. The lawsuit over scholarships follows a May 2023 episode in which Fishback and Whatley appeared to be on the same page in their criticism of the National Speech and Debate Association (NSDA), a rival to Incubate Debate, over censorship. Fishback wrote an essay for The Free Press, then owned by Bari Weiss, the CBS news editor-in-chief, stating that the NSDA had become a “woke” organization “hijacked by left-wing politics” that was telling students what they could and could not talk about. Whatley, then a high school sophomore, told Fox News Digital that she was warned by the organization to refrain from bringing up then former president Donald Trump during debates because it would be “inappropriate”.

title: US House ethics panel recommends censuring North Carolina’s Chuck Edwards
summary: Republican congressman was investigated for untoward and inappropriate advances toward two female staffers
body: The US House of Representatives ethics committee on Monday recommended that Chuck Edwards, a Republican congressman, face censure after determining he “fostered a hostile work environment and engaged in sexual harassment” by giving gifts and lavishing attention on two young female staffers. The bipartisan panel began investigating the second-term North Carolina congressman earlier this year, after receiving complaints about his conduct. In their report, they determined Edwards broke House rules by singling out the two unidentified aides for special treatment that made them uncomfortable and harmed relations with other employees. While the investigation uncovered no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with the staffers or suggested it, his behavior violated provisions in the House code of conduct that prohibit sexual harassment and unwanted advances. The congressman “acknowledged at least some of the behavior at issue could be viewed as inappropriate”, but “has not acknowledged or taken responsibility for the harm he caused”, the committee wrote in its report. “A member of Congress should not single out a staffer and isolate them from other staff, make frequent comments regarding that person’s appearance and weight, send messages in the middle of the night, text staff deeply personal and seemingly romantic thoughts, intrude on personal occasions without invitation, pay for personal vacations, and spend thousands of dollars on gifts for staffers,” they continued. A spokesperson for Edwards did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. If the House agrees to censure Edwards, he would have to stand in the well of the chamber while the text of a resolution rebuking him is read aloud. The congressman was already viewed as vulnerable to losing re-election to his western North Carolina district in the November midterm elections. Last week election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball announced it was rating his race a “toss-up” in a sign of improving Democratic chances. “My heart goes out to the young women who took these roles to serve our community,” his Democratic opponent, Jamie Ager, said following the report’s release. “We deserve leaders with the moral character western North Carolina can be proud of.” Elected in 2022 after ousting the scandal-plagued Madison Cawthorn in the Republican primary, Edwards, a former state senator, left most of the hiring for his new office up to his chief of staff, but insisted on bringing “three young women” into his operation, according to the report. This group included a woman who was still in college and identified by the committee as “Staffer 1” and a second in her early 20s, identified as “Staffer 2”. “Both young women were subject to increasingly unusual attention from the congressman while they worked for him, creating an environment where both they and their coworkers felt uncomfortable,” the committee found. These behaviors included Edwards bringing Staffer 1 to a White House event without telling the rest of his staff, buying her flowers and texting her in advance that he was “so excited about tonight” and wanted it to be “perfect”. After the event, the staffer said Edwards tried to “pressure” her into continuing the night together, which the congressman told the committee he did not recall. He invited both staffers to private dinners, and at one point told Staffer 2 to ensure the event was not put on his calendar by his office scheduler. He would also send both “personal texts” later in the evening about planning events together or expressing “personal sentiments”, the committee found. He also planned lengthy and elaborate trips with the two staffers either together or individually, at one point suggesting to Staffer 2 that they “go to Annapolis for lunch, meditate by its water, stroll about town, find a day spa, see a movie, or wipe out the casino”. “I’m probably over thinking being impulsive but I really want you to enjoy our time together nearly as much as [I] know [I] will,” he wrote in a text message to the staffer released by the committee. The behavior made the two staff members uncomfortable, and when a senior employee of his office spoke to Edwards on their behalf, that staffer told the committee the congressman “got very angry” and said she “didn’t understand the unique relationship” he had with the two women. Both staffers later resigned because of his behavior, but gave Edwards other reasons why when they departed. The behavior impacted the morale of his office, the committee found, with one senior aide telling investigators Edwards “lashes out at everyone on the team except” the two women. The congressman denied yelling at his staff. Another staffer said they had told Edwards that an “unfair standard existed” in his office, which he said was caused by employees being “jealous”. Even after she left his employment, Staffer 2 agreed to a trip to Las Vegas with Edwards, saying she felt pressured to do so in part because he had influence over her being hired for another job in civil service. He paid for her flights, accommodation at the Bellagio hotel and a show at the Sphere. After receiving a bouquet of flowers upon arrival, Staffer 2 texted Edwards: “I’m almost ready and just got the flowers – they’re very pretty. Thank you! I did want to flag that the message made me uncomfortable. Just want to make sure this trip isn’t meant to be anything it’s not?” “Understood, and agree. I’m sorry it made you uncomfortable. Nothing was meant by it, other than what was intended to be a cute play on the name of the arrangement,” Edwards responded.

title: ‘Completely hollow’: critics denounce Blanche deal to halt Trump slush fund
summary: Democrats say agreement – which clears way for Blanche’s confirmation – makes promises president can easily reverse
body: A compromise between Todd Blanche and two Republican senators that potentially cleared the way for Blanche’s confirmation as attorney general is weak, Democrats and several experts said, as it makes promises Donald Trump can easily reverse. Blanche, the acting attorney general, posted two documents on Sunday evening showing he was withdrawing an 18 May order allowing for the creation of a $1.8bn weaponization fund and clarifying that broad tax immunity the justice department granted to Trump only applied retroactively to the president, his sons, and businesses. The agreement stemmed from a deal worked out with senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, two Republicans who had threatened to block Blanche’s nomination. Cornyn and Tillis said on Monday they would support Blanche when his vote comes up for the Senate judiciary committee Tuesday. “We are pleased that the Department of Justice has issued a formal order terminating the anti-weaponization fund,” Cornyn and Tillis said. “Additionally, the department has acknowledged in a binding written order that the audit settlement is limited to the plaintiffs and the scope does not extend beyond the defendants in the lawsuit, the IRS and the treasury, addressing concerns that multiple of our Republican colleagues share.” But legal experts and Democrats said what Blanche announced Sunday was far from ironclad and left room for Trump to resurrect the fund. “These assurances are not worth the paper they’re written on,” Brandon DeBot, policy director at the Tax Law Center at NYU, said in a statement. “They don’t pull back on the ongoing attempts to give the president, his family, and his affiliates unauthorized immunity from tax audits. They don’t do anything new to stop the president from trying to bring back the fund, as he threatened to this weekend. It’s abundantly clear we need congressional action.” The documents Blanche released only say the prior justice department order creating the weaponization fund is rescinded. It does not modify the original settlement agreement creating the fund, reached as the result of a Trump lawsuit seeking billions in damages for the unauthorized release of his tax returns. Blanche acknowledged during his confirmation hearing that Trump or his sons – the plaintiffs in the case – could theoretically sue to enforce the agreement. Trump spent the weekend praising the slush fund, and even threatened to revive it. Trump again praised the fund on Monday, saying: “These people were treated so horribly, and this fund could’ve given them some solace.” He added that he had not seen Blanche’s agreement. “I don’t know what they agreed to,” he said. Jamie Raskin, the ranking Democrat on the House judiciary committee, said Blanche’s announcement does nothing to prevent the justice department and Trump from creating the weaponization fund under a different name. Raskin said: “These hollow words are an affront to the American people, Congress and the courts, and are clearly designed to lull Senators Cornyn and Tillis into a false sense that their legitimate concerns have been addressed while leaving Blanche’s corrupt scheme fully intact.” Even if the department does not move ahead with the fund, there is another path for January 6 defendants to receive a payout from the federal government. A once-obscure process under the Federal Tort Claims Act allows anyone to seek damages from the federal government, first by filing a claim and then through a lawsuit. The justice department has wide discretion over whether to settle those lawsuits and some January 6 defendants are already moving through the process with claims for millions of dollars. “This supposed ‘deal’ doesn’t prevent payouts to violent insurrectionists in the future,” Adam Schiff, a California Democrat and member of the senate judiciary committee, said in a post on X. “It doesn’t prevent the admin from bringing the slush fund back from the dead next week or using DOJ’s Judgment Fund for the same illicit purpose.” Republicans and Democrats have harshly criticized the weaponization fund and the tax immunity deal ever since they were announced in mid-May. Both arose out of a $10bn lawsuit Trump, his sons, and business filed against the government for damages over the unauthorized release of his tax returns. The justice department did not even attempt to defend the government in the lawsuit. A federal judge later said it was a “bad-faith” suit designed to engineer a beneficial result for Trump. The New York Times reported in May that the tax immunity could potentially free Trump of a $100m penalty related to past audits of his tax returns. The fund would have been run by five commissioners, four of whom would have been appointed by the attorney general (the fifth would have been named in consultation with congressional leadership). The fund was not required to disclose how much money it paid and to whom and aside from Trump and his sons, there were no restrictions on who could apply. The agreement Blanche announced is “completely hollow”, said Virginia Canter, chief counsel and director of ethics and anti-corruption at Democracy Defenders Action. “Nothing changes the terms of the actual settlement agreement, which cannot be modified without all parties’ consent. As a result, Blanche could reverse course tomorrow if he wanted.” Lawyers for the watchdog group Democracy Forward, which sued over the fund and secured a court order stopping it, sent a letter to the justice department on Monday noting Blanche had still declined to say under oath that the fund was not moving forward. The organization also asked the justice department whether it would seek to amend the underlying settlement agreement. “The DoJ and Acting Attorney General Blanche appear to want to have their cake and eat it too,” Skye Perryman, the group’s president, said in a statement. “They ask members of the United States Senate to believe the anti-weaponization fund is dead while they seek to preserve favor with the president through refusing to make real commitments backed up in court regarding the operation and future of the fund.” Even some Trump allies appeared unpersuaded that Blanche’s announcement amounted to the death of the fund. Mike Howell, an ally of Trump and director of the Oversight Project, a conservative watchdog group, posted a picture of Blanche’s documents on X and said they “can be undone after Tuesday. The weaponization fund is great.”

title: Why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint and how were so many people able to cross from Morocco?
summary: An estimated 50,000 people attempted the journey to the Spanish territory in chaotic and dangerous scenes that resulted in dozens of deaths
body: What has happened and where? Border controls between Morocco and the tiny Spanish territory of Ceuta appeared to break down in the past week, allowing tens of thousands of people to cross on to the Spanish side in chaotic and dangerous scenes that resulted in dozens of deaths. The number of arrivals was more than two-thirds the size of the ordinary population in Ceuta, where a humanitarian crisis was playing out on Friday. Spanish officials said on Monday that an estimated 69,500 people who had arrived late last week in Ceuta had returned to Morocco. As of Monday, about 2,500 people who had made the crossing were believed to still be in Ceuta. Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish territory 400km (250 miles) to the east along north Africa’s Mediterranean coast, constitute the EU’s only land borders with Africa. In Spanish possession since 1580, Ceuta is home to a mixed population of Christians and Muslims, while its Spanish and Moroccan residents and day workers live in relative harmony. Morocco does not officially recognise Ceuta and Melilla as Spanish territories and often refers to them as occupied lands. Why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint? Spain is a main point of arrival into Europe for people seeking better economic opportunities or an escape from violence in their home countries. Ceuta and Melilla are heavily fortified as they are seen as destinations for those trying to reach Spain from Morocco and other parts of Africa. Many migrants who reach Ceuta or Melilla are immediately turned back, but others are held in migrant shelters while they apply for asylum in Spain. To reach Ceuta, people often swim from the Moroccan town of Fnideq, covering about 3 miles (5km). Others attempt the crossing from the nearer town of Belyounech. In 2022, 23 people were killed as about 2,000 people, mostly from sub-Saharan Africa, attempted to cross into Melilla from Morocco, while in 2014 at least 14 people died off Ceuta when 200 people tried to enter by climbing the border fence or swimming around the breakwater that separates the city from Moroccan territory. Migrant arrivals to Ceuta and Melilla are generally much lower than those reaching Spain through the Canary and Balearic islands. Spain’s overall immigrant population has grown considerably in recent decades, with about 10 million people in the country of 50 million having been born elsewhere. Many are from Colombia, Venezuela and Morocco and work in key sectors of the Spanish economy including agriculture, tourism and the services sector. Since at least the mid-1990s, thousands of people cross the Mediterranean each year from north African countries and Turkey in search of asylum in Europe. According to figures from the International Organization for Migration, 35,153 migrant deaths and disappearances have been recorded in the Mediterranean since 2014, with 1,493 dead or missing during the first seven months of 2026. Why were so many people able to cross over? Spanish intelligence sources told El País that the roots of the influx probably lay in a hoax that had swiftly spread across social media after a Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily deported. As the hoax gained steam online, Moroccan border surveillance dwindled to a minimum until it was completely lifted late last week, allowing tens of thousands of people through. However, the crossing could be linked to the rivalry between Morocco and Algeria, and a recent trip by the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, to Algiers. The last mass border crossing, in May 2021, took place after Morocco loosened border controls during a diplomatic row with Spain over Spain’s decision to allow the leader of the Western Sahara independence movement, the Polisario Front, to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain. Morocco and the Polisario Front both lay claim to Western Sahara, which was under Spanish rule until 1975, when colonial authorities handed over the territory to Morocco and Mauritania. That diplomatic crisis ended in 2022 when Madrid reversed its longstanding policy of neutrality and backed Morocco’s plan for Western Sahara – a move that had caused a diplomatic rift between Madrid and Algiers, which supports the Polisario group. Sánchez visited Algiers on 20 July – the first such visit by a Spanish head of government in four years – marking a thaw in relations with Algeria. Matteo Villa, a migration researcher at the Italian Institute for International Political Studies, said politics was most likely involved. “What happened in 2021 was the small-scale version of what happened [on Friday],” he said. “I mean, 50,000 people do not come overnight when usually it’s hundreds per month. Sánchez going to Algeria is something Morocco didn’t really like.” Villa suggested Morocco may have loosened the border as a way of showing it has “the upper hand”, especially because authorities there know it would cause an overreaction in Europe. “They love seeing all the fighting between European countries,” he added. How have governments and authorities reacted? Spain deployed its armed forces and additional police to restore order after the breach, which Sánchez described as “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”. Images and footage of the border chaos sparked a crisis for the Spanish government and divisions within the EU, where rightwing politicians blamed the incident on Spain’s policy of legalising hundreds of thousands of irregular migrants this year. Italy’s far-right government went so far as to call for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone – even though Ceuta and Melilla do not fall under Schengen arrangements in the usual way – while France tightened its borders with Spain.

title: Nolan Wells death: at least two people charged over alleged threats to officials
summary: Threats come as questions surround death of Mississippi teenager, who was found dead after boat trip with friends
body: Several people with no apparent connection to the Nolan Wells case have been criminally charged with making threats amid questions surrounding the Mississippi teenager’s death in July. The death of the 18-year-old Mississippi college freshman has drawn widespread attention since he was found dead following a boat trip to Horn Island, several miles off the Mississippi Gulf coast, with a group of friends. Wells’s death has also heightened racial tensions: Wells was Black and three friends he was with were white. The case has prompted speculation on social media, with users questioning whether Wells’s death could have been racially motivated, as well as claims of defamation amid the investigation into the case. In the weeks since Wells’s death, several threats have been made against Mississippi public officials. One case centers on allegations against Michelle Francine Edwards of Cincinnati, Ohio. She has been charged with one count of transmitting a threatening communication in interstate commerce. According to court records, Edwards used a blocked number to call the chancery clerk’s office in George county – which includes Horn Island – approximately 21 times in July. “Do not go outside,” Edwards allegedly said during those calls. She also allegedly said “the clock is ticking” and “die”. Court records also allege Edwards made several calls to the sheriff’s office in Jackson county, Mississippi. During those calls, Edwards allegedly said, “Y’all got a bomb outside, don’t come outside bitch,” before later asking: “Y’all still in there?” The alleged calls prompted authorities to place the building on lockdown while canine units conducted a bomb sweep. If convicted as charged, Edwards could face a maximum penalty of five years in prison, a $250,000 fine, and three years of supervised release. A separate case centers on allegations against Joseph Alfredo Vasquez Dumarce, from Sacramento, California. Vasquez was arrested on the same charge as Edwards after allegedly threatening chancery judge Ashlee Cole, whose son had been on the boat trip with Wells. According to court documents and screenshots Cole posted online, a Facebook account traced to Dumarce sent her a message that read: “There will be a package coming to your guys office in the next few days. It’s gonna blow you away when you see it.” The post used an acronym for “laughing at loud” and added: “Probably best to have the boys there to see as well. “Blood. So much blood everywhere. Hard to clean. Especially from a boat. But yours will be quick I promise. I got all you info. Not even the FBI can stop this. Once that package is opened, the timer will start.” In response to the messages, the judge said on Facebook: “We realize that the truth will not stop the calls for the death of our small children … We also want to know what happened to Nolan. We will do everything within our power to assist Nolan’s family in their quest for answers.” An independent autopsy performed in July listed Wells’s cause and manner of death as “undetermined, pending investigation”, his family’s lawyer, the civil rights attorney Ben Crump, said. According to Crump, the independent autopsy – paid for by the former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick – found missing neck tissue and unexplained “red discoloration” on the back of Wells’s head. Black civil rights leaders have called for greater transparency and demanded answers in Wells’s case. Speaking at Wells’s funeral, which was paid for by film-maker Tyler Perry, the civil rights leader the Rev Al Sharpton said: “For an 18-year-old young man to no longer be with us, we want answers, not bias either way – just answers … I think that for the family, the closure can come if there is justice. “He was not on that island by himself: somebody saw something and knows something.” Meanwhile, as of Monday, an online fundraiser for some of Wells’s friends had collected about $94,000 for the purpose of defending against any potential litigation in connection with the case. “Instead of being allowed to mourn, what followed was an unprecedented online campaign of accusations, harassment, threats and defamation,” the online fundraiser said. Wells’ official state autopsy has been completed, officials told NBC. But the results of the autopsy by the Mississippi’s state medical examiner’s office have not been released, with them first being sent to a grand jury investigating Wells’s case. The Guardian has contacted the state medical examiner’s office for comment.

title: Fresh US-Iran talks are ‘last chance’ for Tehran to avoid war escalating, Trump says
summary: US president expects negotiations to begin in next day or two but Iran says it is not reviving talks with Washington
body: New talks between Washington and Tehran are the “last chance” for Iran to forge a deal and avoid an escalation of US strikes on the country, Donald Trump said on Monday. Trump said he expected negotiations to begin in the next day or two to reopen the strait of Hormuz and create a pathway for Iran to address the US’s concerns about its nuclear programme. “The first phase is the opening of the straits. The second phase will be the denuclearisation,” he told reporters in the Oval Office. “And that will take a little while.” Trump reiterated that he was running out of patience with Iran. “This is the last chance for them to sign a good document.” Iran has been in discussions with Oman about the creation of a temporary route through the strait that would allow commercial shipping to resume, but is not yet reviving talks with the US, Tehran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said earlier on Monday. Esmail Baghaei denied claims by Trump that talks between the two sides covering all the major disputes between them could restart as early as Monday. “We are not currently negotiating with the United States,” he said. Trump claimed he had held off from launching the biggest strike on any country “since world war two” over the weekend after Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, rang him to urge diplomacy. Trump said the cancellation was conditional on Iran reaching a deal quickly. It is thought to be the 12th time in the war between the US and Iran that Trump has called off threatened strikes. On Monday, the US president called the Iranian leadership “unbelievably duplicitous” in a post on social media. “They ask for a meeting, some would say ‘beg’, talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they’re not having any discussions, that nothing is being talked about, and they’re only dealing with ‘Oman’. They then go on to give their usual blather in saying, the Strait of Hormuz will be operated powerfully by them, when it is already completely controlled by the United States Navy and our ‘Blockade’.” A middle route through the strait would represent progress. Iran is claiming full sovereignty over the strait and has been making demands over its routes and future management, including the possibility of charging fees in return for providing ships with maritime services. One proposal is to create a joint Omani-Iranian company that would provide all the services that insurance companies used to provide at high costs, but at lower prices, and with preferential tariffs for some countries. Unlocking a mutually acceptable route through the strait is the precondition to unlocking all the other agreements laid out in the memorandum of understanding, the ceasefire document both sides signed on 18 June. Disagreements about the memorandum’s obligations has led to a resumption of the war, which has spread to the Red Sea and to Iraq. Last week, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, said Tehran was demanding that ships entering the strait take a route to the north close to Iran, but that some ships could take a southern route. Iran rejected the traffic being divided evenly between the two routes, and also that a third country could start de-mining the routes. Baghaei told a press conference in Tehran: “We are now talking about a corridor that will have a round trip route, not two or three separate routes. This intermediate route is to be used temporarily until a decision is made on a fixed route.” He framed the route as an alternative to the transport separation scheme, the longstanding prewar route overseen by the UN’s International Maritime Office. He said maps had been exchanged by the two sides. Baghaedi said an agreement on a route would not solve all the problems, pointing to the continuing US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, and that unless the US approach changed, there would be no significant improvement in the situation in the strait. Recently there had been gloom in Omani circles about reaching an agreement with Iran on routes, leading to a revival of preparations for Oman’s European allies to start to clear the southern route of mines, a step that might have provoked direct conflict between Iran and European powers. In a sign of the pressure Tehran diplomats face, a statement from the Assembly of Experts, the body of clerics that elects the supreme leader, warned against investing any trust in the US, saying: “Hope for understanding and agreement with this bullying regime will lead nowhere.” However, the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, said he believed the “memorandum of understanding would prove to be the centre of gravity of our foreign relations in the future”. The Saudis’ intervention came in a week in which Riyadh attacked Iranian-backed forces inside Iraq and raised the temperature in its dispute with the Iranian-backed Houthis in northern Yemen, underlining the extent to which Saudi Arabia fears the consequence of an all-out US war against Iran spiralling out of control across the Middle East. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: Athens suitcase death: suspect admits hiding body but denies murder
summary: Police are focusing on Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s final hours in hope of discovering motive for her killing
body: Greek authorities are investigating what may have motivated a 26-year-old Afghan man to kill a Scottish charity worker found dead in a suitcase in an abandoned building in Athens last month. Inquiries have focused increasingly on Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s last few hours alive and police believe they hold the key to revealing why the 38-year-old was targeted. On Sunday the suspect, identified as Sharif Ahmadzai, was accused of intentional homicide after three days of questioning. He will appear before an investigating magistrate to be formally charged on Wednesday. George Kalliakmanis, the honorary president of the police officers’ association in Athens, told the Guardian the homicide division was now intent on discovering the motive behind “the murder” because the Afghan was continuing to deny any role in it, although he had confessed to hiding Ross in a suitcase. “He has admitted to carrying her body in a trolley to the site. Police have CCTV footage of him doing this on the night of 16 July. He has also confessed to withdrawing €10,000 from ATMs using credit cards that belonged to her. But he has denied murder which police do not believe,” Kalliakmanis said. The Afghan, a professional boxer in the lightweight division, is believed to have arrived in Greece via the island of Lesbos as a child refugee at the height of Europe’s migration crisis 10 years ago. He has been quoted as telling police he discovered Ross’s lifeless body in the first floor flat of an apartment block he helped manage in Exarchia, a bohemian district in downtown Athens popular among leftists, foreigners and NGOs. Ahmadzai, who married a US citizen and devout Christian, Alaina Hall, in 2023, had keys to the flat where their own refugee solidarity group, Love Every Nation, regularly met. Investigators have confirmed that Ross, a friend of Hall’s with similar volunteering experience and religious views, had moved to the apartment on 10 July after staying with Greek friends and arriving the capital from Edinburgh on 26 June. Her last telephone call was made from her mobile phone on the night of 15 July – three days before her body was discovered by a homeless man in an abandoned building in Kypseli, about two miles away. Two possible scenarios in the run up to Ross’s death were being studied, police said. “We believe there was a confrontation,” said one source. “But that was spurred by Ross discovering the Afghan rummaging through her things and stealing her credit cards, or was it a case of sexual assault or the Briton spurning his advances?” Forensic scientists believe Ross was “likely asphyxiated” after an initial on-site postmortem, which showed there were no evident signs of injuries on her body. However, the autopsy was also deemed inconclusive because of advanced decay. Further toxicological tests and analysis of vital organs are expected to determine the exact cause of death in the coming days. Hall, who met Ahmadzai on Lesbos, is widely described as having played a “significant role” in the investigation. After allegedly becoming suspicious of Ahmadzai’s movements – and newfound wealth, the result of making cash withdrawals with Ross’s credit cards – she reportedly contacted the police, handed over cash he had given her and moved into a hotel. Adding to the mystery that has engulfed the inquiry, Ross’s phone was used for several days after her death, with text messages sent to family and friends. The messages were described as “deliberately misleading” by police, who believe they were sent in a bid to delay Ross being declared missing. One spoke of her “need to be alone”. “The Afghan’s partner was very helpful,” said Kalliakmanis. “From the day the victim was identified the investigation faced several challenges but thanks to the homicide division being so thorough they cracked it.” Police, who collaborated with the UK’s National Crime Agency and the Scottish service, combed through CCTV footage from cameras in the area where the suitcase was found and from banks where cash withdrawals were made before identifying the suspect.

title: ICE detainee reveals video of drinking water apparently contaminated with worm-like creatures
summary: ‘Disturbing’ footage shared by California detainee surfaces amid wider complaints about conditions in ICE detention
body: Attorneys for a man detained in a California immigration detention center have released footage showing him holding up a bottle of water from inside the facility that appeared to be contaminated with worm-like creatures. The footage came from a video call with Carlitos Ricardo Parias, a Los Angeles man who has been detained for months at the Adelanto Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility, north-east of LA. Margaret Hellerstein, one of Parias’s attorneys, shared the footage with the Guardian on Thursday and said it was filmed this week. The clip is brief and grainy, but shows him holding up a plastic bottle filled with water, which appeared to have small pests of some kind swimming inside. Parias, in a statement shared by Hellerstein, described them as “worms” or some kind of “larvae”, though it’s unclear what exactly was in the bottle. He said the water was given to residents to drink. The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to repeated questions about the video, with a spokesperson saying in an email that the facility gets its water from the city of Adelanto and provides the “the same water used by residents and businesses in the area”. Geo Group, the private prison company that runs the ICE facility, did not respond to inquiries. The footage has surfaced weeks after a federal judge ordered ICE to ensure that people detained in Adelanto had “24-hour access to clean, potable drinking water”. The ruling was a response to a class-action lawsuit challenging “dangerous conditions” at Adelanto, with detained plaintiffs alleging they were denied sufficient food, clean drinking water and proper medical care. Parias said in his statement that the contaminated water came from jugs that staff had given residents for drinking. He said he poured the water with the worms into a bottle to preserve it as evidence. He showed the bottle to a relative on a video call, which was shared with his attorneys. “This is what they give us: contaminated water, water with larvae, water with little black worms, which is slowly killing each one of us who are detained here,” Parias said in his statement, which his lawyer translated from Spanish. “We need proper drinking water, better treatment.” The exact source of the water in the footage was not clear, and it also was not clear how widely this water was distributed to residents in the detention center. Parias is a TikTok creator known as Richard LA. He received national attention after he was shot by an ICE agent in October and then charged with assault. A federal judge dismissed the charge and he was transferred to ICE custody where he is facing removal. “When I saw the video, I was horrified and disgusted. I felt sick to my stomach,” said Hellerstein. “This is video evidence. They can’t just sweep it under the rug.” The footage has circulated widely among advocates and immigration attorneys in recent days. Lawyers involved in the class-action case said they had seen the footage, but also had not heard direct accounts from other detained residents about the specific contaminant shown in the video. “The video is very disturbing and we’re looking into it,” said Rebecca Brown, supervising attorney at Public Counsel, a public interest law firm that brought the lawsuit, alongside several other organizations. “Detained individuals have long complained about the quality of the water … We’ve heard of water being murky, tasting terrible, having unknown things in it.” Carl Bergquist, counsel with the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, another group representing the class-action plaintiffs, said the footage was concerning and raised questions about whether the government was complying with the judge’s order to provide clean water. The class-action lawsuit said the tap water at the facility was “discolored and tastes odd, raising serious concerns about its potability”, with lawyers writing: “The ‘drinking’ water provided in coolers often appears dirty and regularly runs out for hours at a time.” The judge’s recent order called for consistent water access and improvements to other standards. In a filing challenging the judge’s order this week, lawyers for DHS said the drinking water had been “sampled and tested at various distribution points by an independent third party … and determined to be clean per Food and Drug Administration (FDA) standards”. DHS has also argued in court that Geo Group as a contractor is responsible for the conditions of the facility. Geo Group is not a defendant in the lawsuit.

title: Letter: Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani obituary
summary: Andrew M Rosemarine writes: Passport confiscation for the large numbers of migrant workers was commonplace
body: The reign of Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani as emir of Qatar, from 1995 to 2013, was controversial. Although around 88% of Qatar’s residents were and remain foreign workers, laws intended to protect them were rarely enforced. Passport confiscation for the large numbers of migrant workers was commonplace, as were human trafficking and overcrowded and unsanitary labour camps. The emir arbitrarily made more than 5,000 Qataris of the Ghufran clan stateless, depriving them of state jobs, education and healthcare. Some of them stated that this was collective punishment, because some members were involved in a failed coup attempt in 1996. Injustices have continued as a result. In 2012, a Qatari court tried the poet Mohamed al Ajami in secret, and sentenced him to life imprisonment, apparently for criticism of the emir. He had already been held in custody for a year, and was released in 2016, following international pressure. A law punishing criticism of the emir with up to five years’ imprisonment remained in place.

title: Man who returned fire at In-N-Out gunman had done firearm training after 2021 mass shooting
summary: Police credited Jordan Salinas with limiting number of victims in attack on restaurant in Twin Falls, Idaho
body: A healthcare worker returning fire on a 24-year-old gunman who killed three people and wounded several others an In-N-Out Burger in Twin Falls, Idaho, has said his impulse to confront the attacker was “automatic” and “mechanical”. That description from 35-year-old Jordan Salinas came in an interview with the Idaho Statesman that was published on Sunday, providing a detailed account of actions that police credited with limiting the number of victims in the attack a day earlier. Salinas said he was headed out for a horseback riding date with his girlfriend when they stopped at the burger restaurant for lunch at about 2.30pm on Saturday. Salinas saw people fleeing and heard the “pop-pop-pop” of gunfire, according to what he told the Statesman. He said he ran toward the sound in an “automatic” and “mechanical” response, drawing from a shoulder holster a semi-automatic pistol with a suppressor fixed to its barrel. Salinas said he had been training with firearms seriously since a deadly shooting at a mall in Boise, Idaho – about a two-hour drive from Twin Falls – left two dead and four wounded. One of those killed was identified on Monday from social media posts by loved ones as 23-year-old Ashley Garibay, of Stockton, California. Garibay was an employee at the newly-opened outlet of the restaurant chain. Salinas said he watched on Saturday as an attacker later identified as Chad Williams, standing by the drive-through window, lifted a rifle to his shoulder and fired toward cars. Salinas countered by raising his pistol with both hands and firing. “He did not like it when bullets started firing both ways,” Salinas told the outlet. Police later said the attacker died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound, crediting Salinas and an off-duty officer for diverting the shooter with return fire. “We believe their actions helped drive the suspect away from the scene, preventing further casualties,” said Matthew Hicks, the Twin Falls police chief, at a news conference. “We want to take a moment and commend the actions of the off-duty officer and the citizen – and their heroic action to stop this incident.” Jack Johnson, the Twin Falls county sheriff, said: “These people are true heroes in our community. They diverted the shooter and without a doubt saved many lives.” Williams, 24, killed three victims before dying by his own hand, police said. Police added that he wounded seven others at the recently opened restaurant in the southern Idaho city of about 56,000 people. Two of the wounded were treated at a hospital and discharged; three were listed as stable; and two were in critical condition. Salinas – a full-time caregiver of his brother, who gets around in a wheelchair – said he felt “no fear” during the confrontation with Williams after following four steps he had learned in firearm training. Those steps, he said, were “observe, orient, decide [and] act”. “There’s a task that needs to be done, and we’re the ones who need to do it,” he told the outlet. The decision to take up firearms training, he said, came after he reasoned that gunmen go after “soft targets”. And a person in a wheelchair, and the aide at his side, would be exactly that, he said. “Everyone says, ‘It’s not going to happen here,’” Salinas said. “But what if it does?” Salinas’s interview and the police’s praise of him came amid a debate over the correct response of bystanders to mass shootings. Some witnesses to Saturday’s attack in Twin Falls were reported to have slowed their cars and shouted at Williams. As of Monday morning, there had been at least 280 mass shootings reported across the US so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive. The archive, a non-partisan resource, defines mass shootings as cases in which four or more victims are shot or wounded. The high numbers of mass shootings annually reported in the US have driven calls for more substantial federal firearms restrictions. But Congress has not implemented such gun control over the years.
